source.title: DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement Learning

output.summary: DeepSeek-R1 asks whether LLM reasoning can be developed by reinforcement learning with minimal human-written reasoning demonstrations. DeepSeek-R1-Zero applies GRPO directly to DeepSeek-V3-Base using only rule-based accuracy and format rewards, with no SFT stage. Its AIME 2024 pass@1 rises from 15.6% to 77.9%, and response length grows as reflection-like behaviours appear. Because R1-Zero reads poorly, mixes languages and is narrow, DeepSeek-R1 adds a multi-stage pipeline: cold-start SFT, reasoning RL with a language-consistency reward, rejection sampling plus SFT on about 800K samples, and a second RL stage with preference reward models. R1 reaches o1-1217-level results on many reasoning benchmarks, and distilling its outputs into smaller models works better than running RL on those smaller models. The paper also reports safety evaluations, failed attempts (PRM, MCTS) and limitations such as reward hacking where no reliable verifier exists.
main_claims: Reasoning ability can be incentivized by pure RL with verifiable outcome rewards, without human-labeled reasoning trajectories or an SFT warm-up (DeepSeek-R1-Zero).
Under RL, R1-Zero's responses lengthen and reflection, verification and exploring alternatives emerge on their own, including an 'aha moment' with a sudden rise in the word 'wait'.

A multi-stage pipeline (cold-start SFT, reasoning RL, rejection-sampling SFT, preference RL) fixes R1-Zero's readability, language-mixing and generality problems and gives DeepSeek-R1 performance comparable to OpenAI-o1-1217 on math and code.
Pure RL depends on reliable verifiers; model-based rewards are prone to reward hacking, so tasks without a verifier still need SFT data and only brief RL.
Distilling R1's reasoning traces into small models beats applying large-scale RL directly to them, though pushing beyond current capability may need stronger base models and larger-scale RL.

R1 has limitations: weak structured output and tool use, overthinking, language mixing outside Chinese/English, prompt sensitivity, little gain on software engineering, and moderate safety without an external risk control system.
background: Large language model pre-training, post-training and supervised fine-tuning (SFT)
Chain-of-thought prompting and few-shot vs zero-shot prompting
Reinforcement learning basics: policy, reward, advantage, KL penalty
Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) and value/critic models
Benchmarks such as AIME, MATH-500, GPQA, Codeforces, LiveCodeBench
Mixture-of-Experts models at a high level

sections.label: motivation-overview
sections.title: Motivation and Overview of the Approach
key_points: Existing CoT and post-training approaches rely on human-annotated reasoning traces, which limits scalability and caps performance at human-style reasoning.
The authors bypass SFT and use GRPO on DeepSeek-V3-Base with rewards based only on final-answer correctness, hypothesising that human-defined patterns limit exploration.
R1-Zero reasons well but has poor readability, language mixing and narrow scope, motivating the multi-stage DeepSeek-R1 and the distilled models.

sections.label: grpo-algorithm
sections.title: GRPO: Group Relative Policy Optimization
key_points: For each question GRPO samples a group of outputs from the old policy and optimizes a clipped objective with a KL penalty to a reference policy.
The advantage is each reward's deviation from the group mean divided by the group standard deviation, so no learned value model is needed.
Training settings for R1-Zero include learning rate 3e-6, KL coefficient 0.001, 16 samples per question, and a max length raised from 32,768 to 65,536 at step 8.2k.

sections.label: grpo-vs-ppo
sections.title: Why GRPO Rather Than PPO
key_points: PPO needs a value model of similar size to the policy, adding memory and compute cost and being hard to train on long reflective CoT with only outcome rewards.
GRPO adds the KL term to the loss rather than as a per-token reward; the authors argue PPO's cumulative KL penalty may implicitly discourage longer responses.
The reference policy is periodically replaced by the latest policy to balance exploration and stability.
On MATH with a small model, PPO with lambda 0.95 is well below GRPO, and tuned lambda 1.0 nearly matches it but needs extra tuning.

sections.label: r1-zero-rewards-results
sections.title: R1-Zero: Rewards, Template and Emergent Behaviour
key_points: The reward is rule-based: accuracy (answer matching or compiler tests) plus format (reasoning inside think tags), equally weighted.
Neural reward models are avoided for reasoning because of reward hacking risk and extra complexity.
The prompt template constrains only structure, not content, so natural progression can be observed.
AIME 2024 pass@1 goes from 15.6% to 77.9%, and 86.7% with self-consistency, above the human average.
Response length grows steadily, reflective words increase 5-7x, and the 'aha moment' (sudden rise in 'wait') is shown, though this is evidenced by word counts and a sample.

sections.label: r1-pipeline
sections.title: DeepSeek-R1 Multi-Stage Pipeline
key_points: Stages: cold-start long-CoT SFT (thousands of samples), reasoning RL with language-consistency reward, rejection sampling plus SFT, then second RL for helpfulness, harmlessness and reasoning.
Helpful reward model trained on 66K preference pairs judged by DeepSeek-V3; safety reward model trained point-wise on 106K prompts.
Language consistency reward is the proportion of target-language words in the CoT; ablation shows slight performance loss but better readability.
The second RL stage uses temperature 0.7, 1,700 steps, with preference rewards only in the last 400 steps to avoid reward hacking; clip ratio matters for stability.

sections.label: data-recipe
sections.title: Training Data: RL Data, Cold Start and the 800K SFT Set
key_points: Reasoning RL data covers math (26K), code (17K), STEM (22K) and logic (15K), all verifiable; general data (66K) uses reward models.
Cold-start data come from filtered R1-Zero outputs rewritten by DeepSeek-V3 and humans into readable, first-person, single-language style.
The SFT set has about 800K samples: roughly 600K reasoning samples from rejection sampling and 200K non-reasoning, mostly single-turn.
The authors caution that readable, human-like reasoning style reflects engineered heuristics rather than human-like intelligence.

sections.label: main-results
sections.title: Main Results and Stage-by-Stage Analysis
key_points: Dev1 improves instruction-following but loses reasoning performance (e.g. AIME) due to the small cold-start set; Dev2 restores reasoning gains after RL.
Dev3 (SFT with reasoning and non-reasoning data) lifts AlpacaEval and Aider-Polyglot; final RL mainly improves general instruction-following and preference benchmarks.
Final R1 scores include AIME 2024 79.8, MATH-500 97.3, Codeforces rating 2029.
Reasoning-oriented RL helps reasoning much more than user-preference benchmarks.

sections.label: evaluation-comparisons
sections.title: Evaluation Setup, Comparisons and Human Baselines
key_points: Pass@1 is estimated from k sampled responses at temperature 0.6 rather than greedy decoding, with k up to 64.
Decontamination uses 10-gram filtering, which cannot catch paraphrases, so older benchmarks may be contaminated.
R1 is on par with o1-1217 on math, behind it on Aider, and comparable on SWE Verified; it beats the human AIME mean and Codeforces 96.3% of participants but trails PhD experts on GPQA.
On ChatbotArena (style control) R1 shares first place at the time of the screenshot.

sections.label: further-analysis
sections.title: Further Analysis: Generalization, Test-Time Compute and Stage Gains
key_points: R1 beats V3 mostly on STEM and reasoning, while V3 keeps an edge in instruction-following (IF-Eval).
On AIME 2025 R1 gets a 75% solve rate, approaching o1's 80%; per-category math results show weakness in geometry and combinatorics.
R1 adaptively spends more thinking tokens on harder problems; majority voting helps GPT-4o little but lifts R1 from 79.8% to 86.7% on AIME 2024.
On LiveCodeBench each stage's gains come mainly from medium and hard problems.

sections.label: distillation-and-key-findings
sections.title: Distillation, Key Findings and Failed Attempts
key_points: Fine-tuning small Qwen and Llama models on the 800K R1-generated samples (SFT only) yields strong results; the 1.5B model beats GPT-4o and Claude-3.5-Sonnet on math benchmarks.
Qwen2.5-32B with large-scale RL matches QwQ-32B-Preview but is clearly beaten by the distilled 32B model.
A sufficiently large base checkpoint is needed for RL to work; small 7B/16B models failed to improve on AIME.
Process reward models and MCTS were tried and abandoned because of step definition, reward hacking and token-level search-space difficulty.

sections.label: safety-limitations
sections.title: Safety, Limitations and Future Work
key_points: R1 can be jailbroken, and its stronger reasoning could make harmful plans more actionable; open weights can be fine-tuned to remove protections.
Safety reports show moderate intrinsic safety, much improved by an external DeepSeek-V3-based risk control system; jailbreak attacks sharply raise R1's unsafe rate without it.
Limitations include structured output and tool use, overthinking, language mixing, few-shot sensitivity and limited software-engineering gains.
Pure RL needs reliable rewards; reward hacking makes tasks like writing hard, so human-annotated SFT data remain necessary there.
